definition: Reticent means hesitant to speak up; keeping one's thoughts to oneself.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word reticent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know reticent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Grandpa stayed reticent about his years at sea; asked directly, he would nod at the horizon and change the subject.
Private is milder than reticent — a few doors politely closed, plenty still shared — while the reticent keep most of their thoughts unspoken as a general habit.
Walled-off goes further than reticent — a reticent colleague still answers when pressed, while a walled-off one lets nothing through at all.

Tight-lipped is the informal twin of reticent, and it usually clamps shut on one subject in particular — the coach goes tight-lipped about the starting lineup. Reticent describes a person's whole manner: answers short, opinions unoffered, on most topics and most days.

Guarded adds wariness to the quiet — a guarded speaker weighs every word for risk, protecting something from listeners who might use it. Reticent needs no threat at all: the silence is a comfortable preference, chosen and kept even among people who are trusted.

Reticent grows from Latin tacere, 'to be silent' — a root English did keep, in tacit (understood without being said) and taciturn (silent by temperament), both taught elsewhere in this course. This card leaves them to their own lessons; notice only that re- adds no repetition here — just silence, thorough and chosen.
Reticent means hesitant to speak up; keeping one's thoughts to oneself.

Three lunches into her first week, all anyone at the workshop knew about Imani was that she kept bees — and that only because a jar of honey had appeared on the break table with a small handwritten label.
Reticent but warm, she answered questions briefly, asked better ones back, and returned to her sandwich.
The crew liked her enormously and knew almost nothing about her.
Reticent is the exact word for Imani, because it means hesitant to speak up, keeping one's thoughts to oneself — the silence is chosen, comfortable, and aimed mostly at her own affairs.
Guarded would imply wariness, something protected; reticence needs no threat at all, only a preference.
Reticent describes people, and their manner, when thoughts stay unspoken: answers short, opinions unoffered.
Tight-lipped is the informal twin, usually about one topic; guarded adds wariness.

Two boundaries matter: reluctant — a cousin in this unit's reference list — is unwillingness to act, while reticence is unwillingness to speak; and recalcitrant, this unit's louder mate, refuses authority outright.
The reticent refuse nothing; they simply are not saying.

When Priya was assigned Marcus Chen as a lab partner, she assumed his silence meant he resented the pairing.
He answered questions in five words or fewer, offered no opinions about anything -- music, professors, the weather -- and ate lunch with a book.
Halfway through the term she noticed the pattern: he was exactly the same with his oldest friends, and none of them seemed to mind.
Marcus was simply reticent, their TA explained -- not hostile, not hiding anything, just built to keep most of his thoughts to himself.
When he finally did volunteer a full sentence -- that her titration technique was the best in the section -- Priya framed the compliment.
